name: Interpreter
intent: Represent the grammar of a small language as classes, so sentences in that language can be evaluated by walking a tree.
scenario: A calculator evaluates formulas written in postfix notation, like "x 3 * 2 +", where x is a variable set at runtime.
problem: A formula arrives as text. Evaluating it with one big function full of string splitting and if/else for each operator works until you add operators, variables or want to show the parsed structure. The logic and the grammar are tangled together.
solution: Give every kind of expression its own class with an interpret(context) method. Terminals (numbers, variables) answer directly. Non-terminals (add, multiply) hold sub-expressions and combine their results. Parsing builds a tree of these objects, and evaluating is a single call on the root.
pain: One function parses and calculates at the same time
A new operator means editing that function
No structure to inspect, print or optimise
Variables and grammar rules are tangled with parsing
benefits: Each grammar rule is one small class
A new operator is a new class, no edits to existing ones
The expression tree can be printed, simplified or evaluated many times
Variables live in a Context passed down the tree
whenToUse: You have a simple, stable grammar: rules engines, filters, search queries, tiny DSLs
You evaluate the same expression repeatedly with different inputs
You want to extend the language by adding classes
whenNotToUse: The grammar is large or complex: use a parser generator
Performance is critical: tree walking is slower than compiled code
An existing expression library already does the job
pitfalls: One class per rule grows unmanageable for big grammars
The pattern does not parse text; you still need a parser to build the tree
Rarely the right tool: often an off-the-shelf parser is better

roles.label: Nonterminal Expression
roles.description: Rules built from other expressions: add, multiply.

roles.label: Context
roles.description: Holds the information expressions need, like variable values.

quiz.question: A pricing page must compute the postfix formula x 3 * 2 + for 1 million different values of x. The first version splits the string and loops over tokens each time. What is the better approach?
options: Parse the text once into a tree of expression objects, then interpret it with a context holding x
Rebuild the tree for each value of x, with the number x written into a new terminal object and the old tree discarded
Keep the string splitter and cache the token array so that it only needs to split once
Generate one class for each of the 1 million values of x so that each is evaluated directly
quiz.explanation: The tree is built once and reused. The variable is looked up in the context, so changing x needs no rebuild. Caching the tokens still leaves a loop with an if chain on every evaluation, and rebuilding the tree each time wastes the point of having one.

quiz.question: A developer writes Number, Add and Multiply expression classes with an interpret method, and a context for variables. They say the system can now evaluate the string "x 3 * 2 +". What is still missing?
options: A visitor on each expression class, since interpret cannot walk the tree on its own
A parser that reads the text and builds the tree of expression objects from it
A separate Subtract class, because every grammar needs at least four operators to work
A singleton Context, otherwise the variables are not visible to the nested expressions
quiz.explanation: The pattern defines how a tree evaluates, not how text becomes a tree. Something has to turn the string into Number, Add and Multiply nodes. Interpret already recurses through the tree, so a visitor is not required.

quiz.question: A product needs a query language with about 200 grammar rules, nested subqueries, operator precedence and helpful syntax error messages. A teammate proposes one expression class per rule using the Interpreter pattern. What is the best advice?
options: Use the pattern, since adding one class for each rule is the intended way to scale a grammar
Use a parser generator or an existing library, and keep Interpreter for small stable grammars
Use the pattern, but write the parser with regular expressions to keep the class count down
Use the pattern, but store the 200 rules in one class with a switch to avoid class explosion
quiz.explanation: Interpreter suits small, stable grammars. At 200 rules with precedence and error recovery, hand-written classes become unmanageable, and tools built for parsing do it better. Regular expressions cannot handle nested subqueries well.
